claim: Dorsal closure is a conserved morphogenetic process in dipterans.
source: Here, we report evidence indicating that dorsal closure, a conserved morphogenetic process in dipterans, evolved as the consequence of rearrangements in epithelial organization rather than signaling regulation.
evidence: The manuscript states this directly in the abstract.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, dorsal closure consists of a two-tissue system where the contraction of extraembryonic amnioserosa and a JNK/Dpp-dependent epidermal actomyosin cable result in microtubule-dependent seaming of the epidermis.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, dorsal closure consists of a two-tissue system where the contraction of extraembryonic amnioserosa and a JNK/Dpp-dependent epidermal actomyosin cable result in microtubule-dependent seaming of the epidermis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information about D. melanogaster dorsal closure.

claim: Dorsal closure in Megaselia abdita is a three-tissue system comprising serosa, amnion and epidermis.
source: We find that dorsal closure in Megaselia abdita, a three-tissue system comprising serosa, amnion and epidermis, differs in morphogenetic rearrangements despite conservation of JNK/Dpp signaling.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding about M. abdita tissue composition.

claim: M. abdita dorsal closure is driven by the rupture and contraction of the serosa and the consecutive microtubule-dependent seaming of amnion and epidermis.
source: In addition to an actomyosin cable, M. abdita dorsal closure is driven by the rupture and contraction of the serosa and the consecutive microtubule-dependent seaming of amnion and epidermis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The evolutionary transition to a reduced system of dorsal closure involves simplification of the seaming process without changing the signaling pathways of closure progression.
source: Our study indicates that the evolutionary transition to a reduced system of dorsal closure involves simplification of the seaming process without changing the signaling pathways of closure progression.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Mechanical forces produced at the cellular level shape tissues during morphogenesis.
source: Mechanical forces produced at the cellular level are known to shape tissues during morphogenesis (see Lecuit et al., 2011, for a recent review).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Molecular motors and cytoskeletal elements generate mechanical forces that cause tissues to deform and change shape.
source: Molecular motors and cytoskeletal elements generate these mechanical forces, which cause tissues to deform and change shape (Mammoto and Ingber, 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The evolution of developmental processes is generally attributed to changes in genetic regulation.
source: The evolution of developmental processes is generally attributed to changes in genetic regulation (see for example, Carroll et al., 2009; Davidson and Erwin, 2006; Peter and Davidson, 2015; Wilkins, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: Epithelial fusion is a fundamental morphogenetic mechanism in animal development where two opposing epithelial sheets are brought together to subsequently seam and result in a single continuous epithelial layer.
source: Epithelial fusion is a fundamental morphogenetic mechanism in animal development where two opposing epithelial sheets are brought together to subsequently seam and result in a single continuous epithelial layer (Jacinto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Dorsal closure in Drosophila melanogaster is a classical model system to study epithelial fusion.
source: Dorsal closure in Drosophila melanogaster (Diptera: Drosophilidae) is a classical model system to study epithelial fusion (Jacinto et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: In D. melanogaster, dorsal closure is promoted by a contractile actomyosin cable forming at the leading edge of the epidermal flanks.
source: This process is promoted by the mechanical action of different players: a contractile actomyosin cable forming at the leading edge of the epidermal flanks, the extraembryonic amnioserosa which covers the dorsal opening and generates contractile forces during epidermal flank advancement, and the eventual seaming of the epidermis through a mechanism involving microtubule-based cellular protrusions (Eltsov et al., 2015; Hutson et al., 2003; Kiehart et al., 2000; Saias et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The extraembryonic amnioserosa covers the dorsal opening and generates contractile forces during epidermal flank advancement in D. melanogaster.
source: This process is promoted by the mechanical action of different players: a contractile actomyosin cable forming at the leading edge of the epidermal flanks, the extraembryonic amnioserosa which covers the dorsal opening and generates contractile forces during epidermal flank advancement, and the eventual seaming of the epidermis through a mechanism involving microtubule-based cellular protrusions (Eltsov et al., 2015; Hutson et al., 2003; Kiehart et al., 2000; Saias et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Seaming of the epidermis in D. melanogaster occurs through a mechanism involving microtubule-based cellular protrusions.
source: This process is promoted by the mechanical action of different players: a contractile actomyosin cable forming at the leading edge of the epidermal flanks, the extraembryonic amnioserosa which covers the dorsal opening and generates contractile forces during epidermal flank advancement, and the eventual seaming of the epidermis through a mechanism involving microtubule-based cellular protrusions (Eltsov et al., 2015; Hutson et al., 2003; Kiehart et al., 2000; Saias et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway plays an essential regulatory role in dorsal closure in D. melanogaster.
source: Genetically, the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway and the transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) family gene decapentaplegic (dpp) play an essential regulatory role in the process (Fernández et al., 2007; Glise and Noselli, 1997; Jacinto et al., 2002; Knust, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) family gene decapentaplegic (dpp) plays an essential regulatory role in dorsal closure in D. melanogaster.
source: Genetically, the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway and the transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) family gene decapentaplegic (dpp) play an essential regulatory role in the process (Fernández et al., 2007; Glise and Noselli, 1997; Jacinto et al., 2002; Knust, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The expression of dpp localizes to the leading edge of the epidermal flanks in D. melanogaster.
source: The expression of dpp localizes to the leading edge of the epidermal flanks and depends on the activity of the D. melanogaster JNK gene (basket, bsk).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about D. melanogaster.

claim: The expression of dpp depends on the activity of the D. melanogaster JNK gene (basket, bsk).
source: The expression of dpp localizes to the leading edge of the epidermal flanks and depends on the activity of the D. melanogaster JNK gene (basket, bsk).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about D. melanogaster.

claim: Embryos lacking bsk activity show downregulation of dpp at the epidermal leading edge in D. melanogaster.
source: Embryos lacking bsk activity show downregulation of dpp at the epidermal leading edge, failure of dorsal closure progression, and a dorsal-open phenotype in the larval cuticle (Glise and Noselli, 1997; Sluss et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Embryos lacking bsk activity show failure of dorsal closure progression in D. melanogaster.
source: Embryos lacking bsk activity show downregulation of dpp at the epidermal leading edge, failure of dorsal closure progression, and a dorsal-open phenotype in the larval cuticle (Glise and Noselli, 1997; Sluss et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Embryos lacking bsk activity show a dorsal-open phenotype in the larval cuticle in D. melanogaster.
source: Embryos lacking bsk activity show downregulation of dpp at the epidermal leading edge, failure of dorsal closure progression, and a dorsal-open phenotype in the larval cuticle (Glise and Noselli, 1997; Sluss et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Activation of the JNK/Dpp signaling pathways promotes the formation and maintenance of the actomyosin cable at the epidermal leading edge in D. melanogaster.
source: At the molecular level, activation of the JNK/Dpp signaling pathways promotes the formation and maintenance of the actomyosin cable at the epidermal leading edge (Ducuing et al., 2015) and, thus, progression of the opposing epidermal flanks toward the dorsal midline where they meet.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: At the final stage of dorsal closure in D. melanogaster, the opposing epidermal flanks 'zipper' or 'seam' through the action of microtubules that align toward the dorsal opening.
source: At the final stage of dorsal closure, the opposing epidermal flanks 'zipper' or 'seam' through the action of microtubules that align toward the dorsal opening and promote the formation of filopodial protrusions at both epidermal leading edges (Jacinto et al., 2002; Jankovics and Brunner, 2006; Millard and Martin, 2008).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Microtubules promote the formation of filopodial protrusions at both epidermal leading edges during dorsal closure in D. melanogaster.
source: At the final stage of dorsal closure, the opposing epidermal flanks 'zipper' or 'seam' through the action of microtubules that align toward the dorsal opening and promote the formation of filopodial protrusions at both epidermal leading edges (Jacinto et al., 2002; Jankovics and Brunner, 2006; Millard and Martin, 2008).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Dorsal closure is a conserved morphogenetic process that occurs in all insects.
source: Dorsal closure is a conserved morphogenetic process that occurs in all insects (Chapman, 1998).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: In most insects, dorsal closure involves three tissues: the embryonic epidermis, an extraembryonic amnion, and a separate extraembryonic serosa.
source: Although in D. melanogaster it involves two tissues, the embryonic epidermis and the extraembryonic amnioserosa, in most insects it involves three: the embryonic epidermis, an extraembryonic amnion, and a separate extraembryonic serosa (Panfilio, 2008; Schmidt-Ott and Kwan, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: M. abdita has been established as a model to study the evolution of developmental processes.
source: The phorid scuttle fly M. abdita (placed in an early branching cyclorraphan lineage) presents a three-tissue system of dorsal closure and has been established as a model to study the evolution of developmental processes (Bullock et al., 2004; Rafiqi et al., 2008; Schmidt-Ott et al., 1994; Stauber et al., 2000; Wotton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Dorsal closure in M. abdita embryos occurs in three distinct phases: (i) serosa rupture and retraction, (ii) serosa contraction and progression of opposing epidermal flanks, and (iii) a dual seaming process to eventually form a fused continuous epidermis.
source: Here, we perform a quantitative characterization of dorsal closure in M. abdita. Combining molecular tools with live imaging, we show that dorsal closure in M. abdita embryos occurs in three distinct phases: (i) serosa rupture and retraction, (ii) serosa contraction and progression of opposing epidermal flanks, and (iii) a dual seaming process to eventually form a fused continuous epidermis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction.

claim: The regulation of dorsal closure in M. abdita involves a conserved role for the JNK/Dpp signaling pathway to form and maintain an epidermal actomyosin cable surrounding the dorsal opening.
source: Despite the significant morphological differences with D. melanogaster, the regulation of dorsal closure in M. abdita involves a conserved role for the JNK/Dpp signaling pathway to form and maintain an epidermal actomyosin cable surrounding the dorsal opening.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction.

claim: Following an actomyosin-dependent contraction of the serosa, two consecutive microtubule-dependent seaming events take place in the amnion as well as in the epidermis in M. abdita.
source: More specifically, we find that following an actomyosin-dependent contraction of the serosa, two consecutive microtubule-dependent seaming events take place in the amnion as well as in the epidermis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction.

claim: Apical microtubule bundles align and extend toward the site of closure in both amnion and epidermis in M. abdita.
source: In both cases, apical microtubule bundles align and extend toward the site of closure suggesting a general epithelial fusion mechanism.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction.

claim: The evolutionary transition from a three-tissue to a two-tissue system of dorsal closure involves changes in the number and sequence of morphogenetic events, rather than changes in the spatio-temporal activity of the main signaling pathways that control closure progression.
source: They indicate that the evolutionary transition from a three-tissue to a two-tissue system of dorsal closure involves changes in the number and sequence of morphogenetic events, rather than changes in the spatio-temporal activity of the main signaling pathways that control closure progression.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the introduction.

claim: The extraembryonic serosa in M. abdita constitutes the outermost extraembryonic layer and envelops the entire embryo before the onset of dorsal closure.
source: The extraembryonic serosa, which constitutes the outermost extraembryonic layer and envelops the entire M. abdita embryo before the onset of dorsal closure (magenta in Figure 1A, A' and and B,B').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1.

claim: Serosa cells in M. abdita have very large nuclei with an average size of 125± 21 µm2.
source: Its cells have very large nuclei (average size 125± 21 µm2, SD, n = 150 cells) and show discontinuous or 'punctuated' DAPI staining (magenta in Figure 1A and A' and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–A' and B–B'').
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements and supported by figures.

claim: Serosa cells in M. abdita show discontinuous or 'punctuated' DAPI staining.
source: Its cells have very large nuclei (average size 125± 21 µm2, SD, n = 150 cells) and show discontinuous or 'punctuated' DAPI staining (magenta in Figure 1A and A' and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–A' and B–B'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: The extraembryonic amnion in M. abdita is one to two cells wide and localizes in between the serosal and epidermal tissues.
source: The extraembryonic amnion, which is one to two cells wide, localizes in between the serosal and epidermal tissues (blue in Figure 1A, A' and and B,B').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1.

claim: Amnion cells in M. abdita have large nuclei with an average size of 77 ± 16 µm2.
source: Its cells also have large nuclei (average size 77 ± 16 µm2, SD, n = 150 cells) and show a more continuous, 'compact' DAPI staining (blue in Figure 1A and A' and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–A' and B–B'').
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements and supported by figures.

claim: Amnion cells in M. abdita show a more continuous, 'compact' DAPI staining.
source: Its cells also have large nuclei (average size 77 ± 16 µm2, SD, n = 150 cells) and show a more continuous, 'compact' DAPI staining (blue in Figure 1A and A' and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–A' and B–B'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: The embryonic epidermis in M. abdita contains numerous small nuclei with an average size of 14 ± 3 µm2 that are tightly packed.
source: The embryonic epidermis, which contains numerous small nuclei (average size 14 ± 3 µm2, SD, n = 150 cells) that are tightly packed (gray in Figure 1A and A').
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements and supported by Figure 1.

claim: The serosa ruptures at T = 25 min (±8 min, SD; n = 15 embryos) after dorsal ridge fusion in M. abdita.
source: Under this time frame, the serosa ruptures at T = 25 min (±8 min, SD; n = 15 embryos) and dorsal closure (seaming of the embryonic epidermal flanks at the dorsal midline, see yellow line in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A'') concludes at T = 74 min (±10 min, SD, n = 15 embryos).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements from time-lapse imaging.

claim: Dorsal closure concludes at T = 74 min (±10 min, SD, n = 15 embryos) after dorsal ridge fusion in M. abdita.
source: Under this time frame, the serosa ruptures at T = 25 min (±8 min, SD; n = 15 embryos) and dorsal closure (seaming of the embryonic epidermal flanks at the dorsal midline, see yellow line in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A'') concludes at T = 74 min (±10 min, SD, n = 15 embryos).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements from time-lapse imaging.

claim: Following serosa accumulation on top of the dorsal opening, serosa cells undergo an apicobasal elongation resulting in the internalization of a large part of the serosa cells into the yolk prior to epidermal fusion in M. abdita.
source: Visualizing the process from an orthogonal view, we observe that following serosa accumulation on top of the dorsal opening, this extraembryonic tissue bends inwards and serosa cells undergo an apicobasal elongation resulting in the internalization of a large part of the serosa cells into the yolk prior to epidermal fusion (Video 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C–C').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Video 2 and figures.

claim: Around 90% of Mab_bsk dsRNA-injected embryos developed to at least germband retraction stage.
source: Around 90% of Mab_bsk dsRNA-injected embryos developed to at least germband retraction stage (821 out of 922 embryos).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers from the experiment.

claim: Mab_bsk RNAi knock-down resulted in a disrupted pattern of Mab_dpp expression including a complete absence of expression at the leading edge of the epidermis.
source: Mab_bsk RNAi knock-down resulted in both a disrupted pattern of Mab_dpp expression (including a complete absence of expression at the leading edge of the epidermis, magenta arrowheads in Figure 2B) and a dorsal-open phenotype in the larval cuticle (magenta arrowheads in Figure 2B') of ~64% of RNAi-injected and developed embryos (528 out of 821 embryos).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Mab_bsk RNAi knock-down resulted in a dorsal-open phenotype in the larval cuticle of ~64% of RNAi-injected and developed embryos.
source: Mab_bsk RNAi knock-down resulted in both a disrupted pattern of Mab_dpp expression (including a complete absence of expression at the leading edge of the epidermis, magenta arrowheads in Figure 2B) and a dorsal-open phenotype in the larval cuticle (magenta arrowheads in Figure 2B') of ~64% of RNAi-injected and developed embryos (528 out of 821 embryos).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers and supported by Figure 2B'.

claim: Serosa rupture and retraction still occur in Mab_bsk RNAi-injected embryos despite a failure of progression of the epidermal flanks.
source: Interestingly, live imaging of RNAi-injected embryos reveals that serosa rupture and retraction still occur (yellow dashed line in Figure 2C–C'' and Video 3), despite a failure of progression of the epidermal flanks (yellow arrowheads in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; note that the embryo from Video 3 and Figure 2C corresponds to the same embryo in Figure 2—figure supplements 1B, 24 hr after RNAi injection).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C and Video 3.

claim: JNK and Dpp signaling regulate progression of dorsal closure in M. abdita but are not required for the regulation of serosa rupture and retraction.
source: In summary, these results indicate that JNK and Dpp signaling regulate progression of dorsal closure in M. abdita as in D. melanogaster embryos but are not required for the regulation of serosa rupture and retraction.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the RNAi experiments.

claim: F-actin and phosphoMyosin accumulate at the leading edge of the epidermis in M. abdita.
source: Both stains showed accumulation at the leading edge of the epidermis (green arrowheads in Figure 3A and B) and at the surface of serosa cells during internalization (red arrowheads in Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A and B.

claim: F-actin and phosphoMyosin accumulate at the surface of serosa cells during internalization in M. abdita.
source: Both stains showed accumulation at the leading edge of the epidermis (green arrowheads in Figure 3A and B) and at the surface of serosa cells during internalization (red arrowheads in Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A and B.

claim: Serosa cell area reduces over time during their accumulation at the dorsal opening, from an average of 212 ± 52 µm2 to 76 ± 18 µm2 to 33 ± µm2 at 20, 30 and 40 min after serosa rupture, respectively.
source: Measurements from time-lapse sequences showed that serosa cell area reduces over time during their accumulation at the dorsal opening, from an average of 212 ± 52 µm2 (SD; n = 20 cells) to 76 ± 18 µm2 (SD; n = 20 cells) to 33 ± µm2 (SD; n = 20 cells) at 20, 30 and 40 min after serosa rupture, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Amnion cells show low levels of actin and myosin, even during late stages of dorsal closure after full serosa internalization in M. abdita.
source: In contrast, amnion cells show low levels of actin and myosin, even during late stages of dorsal closure after full serosa internalization (blue arrowhead in Figure 3A and B, Figure 3C'' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: RNAi knock-down of Mab_bsk strongly reduces the level of actin accumulation at the epidermal leading edge compared to wild-type embryos.
source: RNAi knock-down of Mab_bsk strongly reduces the level of actin accumulation at the epidermal leading edge compared to wild-type embryos (white arrows in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The embryonic epidermal cable is regulated by the JNK/Dpp signaling pathway in M. abdita.
source: This suggests that the embryonic epidermal cable is similar in structure and regulated by the JNK/Dpp signaling pathway in both M. abdita and D. melanogaster embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the RNAi experiments.

claim: Injection of Y-27632 at early stages of M. abdita dorsal closure reduces actomyosin accumulation at the epidermal leading edge compared to wild-type embryos.
source: Injection of Y-27632 at early stages of M. abdita dorsal closure reduces actomyosin accumulation at the epidermal leading edge compared to wild-type embryos (white arrowheads in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The progression of the epidermal leading edge is arrested upon Y-27632 treatment in M. abdita.
source: The progression of the epidermal leading edge is arrested upon treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–D'' and Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures and video.

claim: The internalization of serosa cells is abolished by Y-27632 treatment as observed by the lack of inward bending and apicobasal elongation of this tissue in orthogonal view.
source: The internalization of serosa cells is also abolished as observed by the lack of inward bending and apicobasal elongation of this tissue in orthogonal view (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–E'' and Video 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures and video.

claim: Actomyosin contractility contributes to both the internalization of the serosa and progression of the epidermal leading edge in M. abdita.
source: These observations indicate that actomyosin contractility contributes to both the internalization of the serosa and progression of the epidermal leading edge.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the Y-27632 experiments.

claim: Actomyosin-based cell contraction is taking place mainly at the final stage of retraction and during serosa internalization in M. abdita.
source: Interestingly, the kinetics of serosa retraction in Y-27632-injected embryos seemed less affected during the first half of the process than the second half (purple curve in Figure 3D), suggesting that actomyosin-based cell contraction is taking place mainly at the final stage of retraction and during serosa internalization.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an inference from the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Actomyosin-based contractility within the serosa and the cable surrounding the dorsal opening are required for the progression of dorsal closure in M. abdita embryos.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that actomyosin-based contractility within the serosa and the cable surrounding the dorsal opening are required for the progression of dorsal closure in M. abdita embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the experiments.

claim: In D. melanogaster, microtubules in epidermal cells at the leading edge align in apical bundles parallel to the dorsoventral axis and protrude into stable filopodia.
source: In epidermal cells at the leading edge, microtubules align in apical bundles parallel to the dorsoventral axis and protrude into stable filopodia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about D. melanogaster.

claim: Aligned epidermal microtubules are required for proper epidermal seaming in D. melanogaster.
source: These aligned epidermal microtubules are required for proper epidermal seaming and their depolymerization leads to defects in seaming and incomplete closure in D. melanogaster (Jankovics and Brunner, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Depolymerization of aligned epidermal microtubules leads to defects in seaming and incomplete closure in D. melanogaster.
source: These aligned epidermal microtubules are required for proper epidermal seaming and their depolymerization leads to defects in seaming and incomplete closure in D. melanogaster (Jankovics and Brunner, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Microtubules in the epidermis of M. abdita orient toward the dorsal midline.
source: Staining fixed M. abdita embryos at different stages of late dorsal closure with a β-tubulin antibody, we observed that microtubules in the epidermis also orient toward the dorsal midline (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B) and protrude from the epidermal leading edge (white arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) forming apical bundles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Microtubules protrude from the epidermal leading edge forming apical bundles in M. abdita.
source: Staining fixed M. abdita embryos at different stages of late dorsal closure with a β-tubulin antibody, we observed that microtubules in the epidermis also orient toward the dorsal midline (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B) and protrude from the epidermal leading edge (white arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) forming apical bundles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Epidermal microtubule alignment is maintained throughout epidermal flank advancement and during epidermal seaming in M. abdita.
source: This epidermal microtubule alignment is maintained throughout epidermal flank advancement and during epidermal seaming (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–C''').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Microtubule bundles in the extraembryonic amnion of M. abdita localize apically and orient toward the internalizing serosa.
source: Interestingly, we find a similar alignment of microtubules in the extraembryonic amnion, where microtubule bundles localize apically (Figure 4B') and orient toward the internalizing serosa (blue arrowheads in Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Amniotic cells in M. abdita present an elongated apical cell surface area (285 ± 81 µm2) compared to serosa cells (57 ± 23 µm2).
source: We could observe that amniotic cells present an elongated apical cell surface area (285 ± 81 µm2, SD; n = 12 cells; blue arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) compared to serosa cells (57 ± 23 µm2, SD; n = 108 cells; red arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Both apical microtubule alignment and elongated apical cell surface area in the amnion are maintained during serosa internalization and merging of amnion cells from opposite flanks in M. abdita.
source: Both apical microtubule alignment and elongated apical cell surface area in the amnion are maintained during serosa internalization and merging of amnion cells from opposite flanks (blue arrowheads in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–C').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Amnion microtubule alignment is lost after the opposite amnion flanks meet at the dorsal midline in M. abdita.
source: Amnion microtubule alignment is subsequently lost after the opposite amnion flanks meet at the dorsal midline (blue arrowhead in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1C''.

claim: Upon serosa internalization, the opposing amniotic flanks of M. abdita embryos meet and fuse at the dorsal midline.
source: We observed that upon serosa internalization, the opposing amniotic flanks of M. abdita embryos meet and fuse at the dorsal midline, suggesting an amniotic seaming process (blue-shaded area in Figure 4C,C' and C'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C and Video 6.

claim: Immediately after amniotic seaming occurred, the epidermal flanks progressed dorsally and also seamed on top of the continuous amnion in M. abdita.
source: Immediately after amniotic seaming occurred, the epidermal flanks progressed dorsally and also seamed on top of the continuous amnion (green dashed line in Figure 4C,C' and C'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C and Video 6.

claim: Seaming velocities in the amnion and epidermis are 8.1 ± 2 µm/min and 3.8 ± 1.7 µm/min, respectively, in M. abdita.
source: An estimation of seaming velocities in the amnion and epidermis (8.1 ± 2 µm/min and 3.8 ± 1.7 µm/min, SD, n = 5 embryos, respectively) shows a variation in speed between the two processes that could result from a difference in the mechanical properties of the fusing epithelia or the seaming angle at each canthi.
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements.

claim: Injection of colcemid does not perturb the kinetics of serosa retraction in M. abdita.
source: Injection of colcemid does not perturb the kinetics of serosa retraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), actin accumulation in serosa cells (red arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and B'), straightening of the epidermal leading edge (white arrowheads in Figure 4D), or actin cable formation (white arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and B').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Injection of colcemid does not perturb actin accumulation in serosa cells in M. abdita.
source: Injection of colcemid does not perturb the kinetics of serosa retraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), actin accumulation in serosa cells (red arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and B'), straightening of the epidermal leading edge (white arrowheads in Figure 4D), or actin cable formation (white arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and B').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Injection of colcemid does not perturb straightening of the epidermal leading edge in M. abdita.
source: Injection of colcemid does not perturb the kinetics of serosa retraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), actin accumulation in serosa cells (red arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and B'), straightening of the epidermal leading edge (white arrowheads in Figure 4D), or actin cable formation (white arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and B').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Injection of colcemid does not perturb actin cable formation in M. abdita.
source: Injection of colcemid does not perturb the kinetics of serosa retraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), actin accumulation in serosa cells (red arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and B'), straightening of the epidermal leading edge (white arrowheads in Figure 4D), or actin cable formation (white arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and B').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: The initial inward bending and apicobasal elongation of the serosa cells during internalization occurs in both wild type and colcemid injected embryos in M. abdita.
source: An orthogonal view from a time-lapse sequence also shows that the initial inward bending and apicobasal elongation of the serosa cells during internalization occurs in both wild type and colcemid injected embryos (Video 7 and magenta dashed lines in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–C' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–C').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Video 7 and figures.

claim: Dorsal closure arrests during the internalization of the serosa after colcemid injection in M. abdita.
source: In contrast, dorsal closure arrests during the internalization of the serosa (red arrowhead in Figure 4D'') and does not progress toward epithelial seaming (Video 8 and red curve in Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures and video.

claim: Microtubule polymerization does not occur in colcemid-injected embryos in M. abdita.
source: We observe that microtubule polymerization does not occur in colcemid-injected embryos (blue and white arrowheads for amnion and epidermal cells, respectively, in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D compared to 2D') and that amnion cells initially elongate toward the dorsal midline as in wild-type conditions, although they relax and retract from the amnion merging site (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and Video 9).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Amnion cells initially elongate toward the dorsal midline in colcemid-injected embryos but relax and retract from the amnion merging site in M. abdita.
source: We observe that microtubule polymerization does not occur in colcemid-injected embryos (blue and white arrowheads for amnion and epidermal cells, respectively, in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D compared to 2D') and that amnion cells initially elongate toward the dorsal midline as in wild-type conditions, although they relax and retract from the amnion merging site (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and Video 9).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures and video.

claim: Microtubule depolymerization does not affect amnion cell elongation and dorsal convergence but rather a subsequent amniotic seaming in M. abdita.
source: Thus, microtubule depolymerization does not affect amnion cell elongation and dorsal convergence but rather a subsequent amniotic seaming.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the colcemid experiments.

claim: UV-irradiation of colcemid-treated embryos in a region between the epidermis and the internalizing serosa (corresponding to the amnion) allows dorsal closure to progress further compared to colcemid-treated embryos.
source: In UV-irradiated embryos, dorsal closure progressed further, reducing the height (h) of the dorsal opening, compared to colcemid-treated embryos, although it did not progress to the extent of wild-type control embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton in the amniotic tissue is required for seaming of the amnion and the completion of dorsal closure in M. abdita.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that the microtubule cytoskeleton in the amniotic tissue is required for seaming of the amnion and the completion of dorsal closure.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the experiments.

claim: Opposing amniotic flanks fuse at the dorsal midline upon serosa ingression, followed by epidermal seaming in M. abdita.
source: In summary, the results presented in this section indicate the presence of subsequent microtubule-based seaming processes in both the amnion and the epidermis during dorsal closure in M. abdita. First, opposing amniotic flanks fuse at the dorsal midline upon serosa ingression, followed by epidermal seaming (see schematics in Figure 4F and F' and lower panels of Figure 4—figure supplement 4b–b'').
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Both amniotic and epidermal seaming processes are necessary for the completion of epidermal seaming and dorsal closure in M. abdita.
source: Both processes are necessary for the completion of epidermal seaming and dorsal closure, to result in a continuous embryonic epidermal sheet.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text.

claim: Serosa contraction contributes to bringing amniotic flanks into close proximity in M. abdita.
source: Our results indicate that serosa contraction contributes to bringing amniotic flanks into close proximity and that amniotic seaming is a microtubule-dependent event.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the experiments.

claim: Amniotic seaming is a microtubule-dependent event in M. abdita.
source: Our results indicate that serosa contraction contributes to bringing amniotic flanks into close proximity and that amniotic seaming is a microtubule-dependent event.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the experiments.

claim: Dorsal closure in M. abdita involves three different tissues: the embryonic epidermis, as well as the extraembryonic amnion and serosa.
source: In this study, we provide a detailed characterization of epithelial fusion during dorsal closure in the non-drosophilid scuttle fly M. abdita. In this species, dorsal closure involves three different tissues: the embryonic epidermis, as well as the extraembryonic amnion and serosa.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Genetic regulation of dorsal closure by the JNK and Dpp signaling pathways appears to be conserved between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Even though genetic regulation of dorsal closure by the JNK and Dpp signaling pathways appears to be conserved between M. abdita and D. melanogaster, the sequence of morphogenetic rearrangements is very different between the two species.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: The sequence of morphogenetic rearrangements during dorsal closure is very different between M. abdita and D. melanogaster.
source: Even though genetic regulation of dorsal closure by the JNK and Dpp signaling pathways appears to be conserved between M. abdita and D. melanogaster, the sequence of morphogenetic rearrangements is very different between the two species.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: In M. abdita, the serosa encloses the whole embryo and is apposed to the amnion, which in turn is apposed to the epidermis at the edge of the dorsal opening.
source: In M. abdita, the serosa encloses the whole embryo. It is apposed to the amnion, which in turn is apposed to the epidermis at the edge of the dorsal opening (schematics in Figure 1B and B') (see also Rafiqi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation and reference to figures.

claim: Rupture of the serosa is not triggered exclusively by global straining and non-autonomous forces applied to the serosa tissue in M. abdita.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that rupture is not triggered exclusively by global straining and non-autonomous forces applied to the serosa tissue. Instead, rupture seems to be triggered by a specific localized cue.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on observations.

claim: Rupture of the serosa seems to be triggered by a specific localized cue in M. abdita.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that rupture is not triggered exclusively by global straining and non-autonomous forces applied to the serosa tissue. Instead, rupture seems to be triggered by a specific localized cue.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on observations.

claim: The retracting serosa internalizes into the dorsal opening of M. abdita through an actomyosin-dependent mechanism.
source: Upon rupture, the remaining serosal tissue retracts and constricts dorsally through an actomyosin-dependent mechanism, in a way similar to serosa rupture and retraction in the beetle T. castaneum (Hilbrant et al., 2016; Panfilio et al., 2013). The retracting serosa then internalizes into the dorsal opening of M. abdita.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: A JNK/Dpp-dependent actomyosin cable forms at the epidermal leading edge of M. abdita embryos concomitant with serosal internalization.
source: Concomitant with serosal internalization, a JNK/Dpp-dependent actomyosin cable forms at the epidermal leading edge of M. abdita embryos.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: The actomyosin cable promotes the advancement of the opposing epidermal flanks toward the dorsal midline, and the eventual seaming of the two flanks in M. abdita.
source: It promotes the advancement of the opposing epidermal flanks toward the dorsal midline, and the eventual seaming of the two flanks.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Dorsal closure in M. abdita differs from T. castaneum, where no actomyosin epidermal cable appears to be involved in epidermal flank advancement.
source: This stage of dorsal closure occurs in a similar fashion to D. melanogaster, but differs in comparison with T. castaneum, where no actomyosin epidermal cable appears to be involved in epidermal flank advancement (Panfilio et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Dorsal closure in M. abdita involves an additional amniotic seaming process compared to D. melanogaster.
source: In contrast to D. melanogaster, dorsal closure in M. abdita involves an additional amniotic seaming process.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Amniotic seaming is microtubule-dependent and essential for dorsal closure to occur in M. abdita.
source: Our experimental data indicate that amniotic seaming is microtubule-dependent and essential for dorsal closure to occur.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: The two sequential amniotic and epidermal seaming processes in M. abdita involve a dorsoventral alignment of microtubules.
source: Thus, similar to epidermal seaming in D. melanogaster embryos, where microtubules align dorsoventrally prior to tissue fusion (Jankovics and Brunner, 2006), the two sequential amniotic and epidermal seaming processes in M. abdita also involve a dorsoventral alignment of microtubules.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Shape elongation of amniotic cells toward the retracting and internalizing serosa could promote microtubule reorientation in the direction of contractile cells in M. abdita.
source: One possible scenario is that shape elongation of amniotic cells toward the retracting and internalizing serosa could promote microtubule reorientation in the direction of contractile cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a possible explanation.

claim: Cellular fusion in the developing trachea of D. melanogaster involves cell elongation and microtubules orientation toward the site of fusion.
source: Interestingly, cellular fusion in the developing trachea of D. melanogaster involves cell elongation and microtubules orientation toward the site of fusion (Kato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Elongation of cells toward a contractile tissue occurs during gastrulation in D. melanogaster.
source: Elongation of cells toward a contractile tissue also occurs during gastrulation in D. melanogaster (Rauzi et al., 2015) and neural tube closure in the chordate Ciona intestinalis (Hashimoto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Elongation of cells toward a contractile tissue occurs during neural tube closure in the chordate Ciona intestinalis.
source: Elongation of cells toward a contractile tissue also occurs during gastrulation in D. melanogaster (Rauzi et al., 2015) and neural tube closure in the chordate Ciona intestinalis (Hashimoto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Laser-ablation of epidermal canthi slows down the last stages of dorsal closure in D. melanogaster.
source: In the case of D. melanogaster, laser-ablation of epidermal canthi (i.e. the epidermal corners where opposing epidermal flanks meet) slows down the last stages of dorsal closure (Wells et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: F-actin-enriched epidermal seaming still occurs between the opposing leading edges of the epidermis despite the removal of the canthi in D. melanogaster.
source: However, F-actin-enriched epidermal seaming still occurs between the opposing leading edges of the epidermis despite the removal of the canthi.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge about D. melanogaster.

claim: Dorsal closure in embryos of M. abdita presents two sequential seaming events that share a common feature: transient microtubule reorganization.
source: Dorsal closure in embryos of M. abdita presents two sequential seaming events that share a common feature: transient microtubule reorganization.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: The evolutionary transition from a three-tissue to a two-tissue system of dorsal closure involves the reduction of extraembryonic tissue, for example from distinct amnion and serosa to a fused amnioserosa.
source: Our work suggests that the evolutionary transition from a three-tissue to a two-tissue system of dorsal closure not only involves the reduction of extraembryonic tissue, for example from distinct amnion and serosa to a fused amnioserosa (see Horn et al., 2015; Rafiqi et al., 2008; Rafiqi et al., 2010; Schmidt-Ott and Kwan, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claim: The evolutionary transition from a three-tissue to a two-tissue system of dorsal closure requires changes in epidermal progression and seaming events.
source: Our work suggests that the evolutionary transition from a three-tissue to a two-tissue system of dorsal closure not only involves the reduction of extraembryonic tissue, for example from distinct amnion and serosa to a fused amnioserosa (see Horn et al., 2015; Rafiqi et al., 2008; Rafiqi et al., 2010; Schmidt-Ott and Kwan, 2016). In addition, it requires changes in epidermal progression and seaming events.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion.

claim: In the case of dipteran dorsal closure, the evolutionary modulation of tissue remodeling is mainly driven by morphological rearrangements rather than large changes in gene expression.
source: In the case of dipteran dorsal closure, it appears that the evolutionary modulation of tissue remodeling is mainly driven by morphological rearrangements rather than large changes in gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion.

claim: Devitellinization removes the serosa together with the vitelline membrane in M. abdita embryos at dorsal closure stage.
source: When fixing M. abdita embryos at dorsal closure stage, devitellinization also removes the serosa together with the vitelline membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Devitellinization and serosa cells removal resulted in a gap on the dorsal side of M. abdita embryos.
source: Devitellinization and serosa cells removal resulted in a gap on the dorsal side of the embryo, seen as lack of phalloidin staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Amnion cells remained apposed to an intact epidermis after devitellinization in M. abdita.
source: Amnion cells (1–2 cell rows adjacent to the epidermis, blue arrowheads in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) remained apposed to an intact epidermis.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Serosa and amnion cells are apposed in M. abdita embryos.
source: An optical re-slice of confocal projections of the intact serosa and amnion cells showed that these two cells types are apposed (yellow arrowhead in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2C''.

claim: Serosa rupture initiates close to the posterior pole of M. abdita embryos.
source: Serosa rupture initiates close to the posterior pole of the embryo.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation.

claim: Spread of the serosa rupture occurs anteriorly through the ventral side of M. abdita embryos.
source: Spread of the rupture occurs anteriorly through the ventral side of the embryo and results in a retraction of the serosa toward the dorsal end of the embryo (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: During serosa rupture and retraction, serosa cells accumulate at the dorsal opening in M. abdita.
source: During this process, serosa cells accumulate at the dorsal opening (magenta arrowheads in Figure 1D, and magenta cells in 1 G-G'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D and schematics.

claim: The amnion remains in place, apposed to the serosa, during serosa rupture and retraction in M. abdita.
source: In the meantime, the amnion remains in place, apposed to the serosa (blue arrowheads in Figure 1D, and blue cells in 1 G-G''), and adjacent to the embryonic epidermis (white arrowheads in Figure 1D, and green line in 1 G-G'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D and schematics.

claim: The fusion of the dorsal ridge is used as a developmental landmark for the initiation of dorsal closure (T = 0 min) in M. abdita.
source: We used the fusion of the dorsal ridge (merging of the ridge primordia at the dorsal midline, magenta bar in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and A') as a developmental landmark for the initiation of dorsal closure (T = 0 min) (Campos-Ortega and Hartenstein, 1997; VanHook and Letsou, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations and supported by figures.

claim: At early stages of dorsal closure, the leading edge of the epidermis straightens in M. abdita.
source: At early stages of dorsal closure, the leading edge of the epidermis straightens (yellow line in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and A'') and the dorsal opening increases progressively in height (h) (blue curve in Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: The dorsal opening increases progressively in height at early stages of dorsal closure in M. abdita.
source: At early stages of dorsal closure, the leading edge of the epidermis straightens (yellow line in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and A'') and the dorsal opening increases progressively in height (h) (blue curve in Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1F.

claim: Serosa rupture, retraction and accumulation onto the dorsal opening is concurrent with a fast reduction in dorsal opening height in M. abdita.
source: After dorsal ridge fusion (pink area in Figure 1F), the serosa ruptures, retracts and accumulates onto the dorsal opening (Figure 1C, magenta arrowheads in 1D, yellow dashed line in 1E, magenta cells in 1G'-G''). This is concurrent with a fast reduction in dorsal opening height (red and blue curves in Figure 1F, yellow line in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and A'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Extraembryonic tissues internalize during dorsal closure and do not accumulate underneath the fused epidermis after completion of the process in M. abdita.
source: Optical re-slices of confocal projections along the anterio-posterior axis of fixed embryos show that extraembryonic tissues internalizes during dorsal closure and do not accumulate underneath the fused epidermis after completion of the process (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: At late dorsal closure stages, the serosa is fully internalized in M. abdita.
source: Thus, at late dorsal closure stages, the serosa is fully internalized (magenta cells in Figure 1G'') and the two epidermal flanks continue progressing toward the dorsal midline, covering the dorsal opening and eventually fusing completely (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: The two epidermal flanks continue progressing toward the dorsal midline after serosa internalization, covering the dorsal opening and eventually fusing completely in M. abdita.
source: Thus, at late dorsal closure stages, the serosa is fully internalized (magenta cells in Figure 1G'') and the two epidermal flanks continue progressing toward the dorsal midline, covering the dorsal opening and eventually fusing completely (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: In wild-type M. abdita embryos, Mab_dpp is expressed along the leading edge of the epidermis.
source: Using in situ hybridization and cuticle preparations, we observed that in wild-type embryos, M. abdita dpp (Mab_dpp) is expressed along the leading edge of the epidermis (black arrowheads in Figure 2A) and progression of dorsal closure results in the deposition of a continuous larval cuticle (Figure 2A'), very similar to D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: Progression of dorsal closure results in the deposition of a continuous larval cuticle in wild-type M. abdita embryos.
source: Using in situ hybridization and cuticle preparations, we observed that in wild-type embryos, M. abdita dpp (Mab_dpp) is expressed along the leading edge of the epidermis (black arrowheads in Figure 2A) and progression of dorsal closure results in the deposition of a continuous larval cuticle (Figure 2A'), very similar to D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A'.

claim: Actin-enriched filopodia-like extensions protrude from the actomyosin cable in M. abdita.
source: Closer observation also reveals the presence of actin-enriched filopodia-like extensions protruding from the actomyosin cable (yellow arrowheads in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and C').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Upon serosa internalization, the amniotic flanks move to the dorsal midline where the two flanks merge in M. abdita.
source: A timed sequence of phalloidin-stained M. abdita embryos (Figure 3C–C''') reveals further details concerning the dynamics of dorsal closure: upon serosa internalization, the amniotic flanks (devoid of actomyosin) move to the dorsal midline where the two flanks merge (white arrowhead in Figure 3C'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Upon merging of amnion flanks, the actomyosin cable propels the epidermal flanks to the dorsal midline where epidermal seaming takes place in M. abdita.
source: Upon merging of amnion flanks, the actomyosin cable propels the epidermal flanks to the dorsal midline where epidermal seaming takes place (yellow arrowheads in Figure 3C', C'' and C''').
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C.
